## PHASE: builder
## ISSUE: 243

### Issue Details
## Issue #243

## Parent

#242 ([PRD] Cross-Module Generalization: Customer Component + Full POS Line Items)

## What to build

Extract the customer selector from POS into a shared component at `client/src/features/customers/components/CustomerSelector.tsx` that all four modules (POS, Repairs, Orders, Quotes) can import. The component accepts `{ customerId, onSelect, required }` props and handles search debounce, dropdown rendering, keyboard navigation, and walk-in/anonymous selection uniformly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `CustomerSelector` component created at `client/src/features/customers/components/CustomerSelector.tsx`
- [ ] Props interface: `{ customerId?: string | null, onSelect: (id: string | null) => void, required?: boolean }`
- [ ] Search with 250ms debounce, dropdown results, keyboard navigation (ArrowDown/Up/Enter/Escape)
- [ ] Walk-in/anonymous option always present; selecting it calls `onSelect(null)`
- [ ] POS imports and uses the shared component (old inline version removed from `pos/components/CustomerSelector.tsx`)
- [ ] Unit tests for selection callback, null handling, and debounce behavior
- [ ] No visual or behavioral regression in POS customer selection

## Blocked by

None - can start immediately

## Parent PRD (#242)

## Problem Statement

The four core transaction modules — POS, Repairs, Orders, and Quotes — each implement their own customer selection logic, line item validation schemas, and UI components independently. This creates duplication (~150-200 lines of near-identical search/debounce/dropdown code per module), inconsistent behavior (customer required in some modules but optional in others), and makes cross-module changes error-prone because the same concept is implemented differently four times.

POS currently only supports parts-only line items, making it unable to serve as a reference implementation for the other three modules which already support labor and bicycle line types. The validation schemas are scattered across separate files with no shared variant definitions, meaning any change to how a "part" or "labor" line item works must be replicated manually in up to four different schema files.

## Solution

Make POS the clean reference implementation by:
1. Extracting the customer selector into a single shared component used by all four modules
2. Creating shared line item variant definitions that each module composes into its own validation schema
3. Upgrading POS to support all three line item types (part, labor, bicycle) matching the domain model already present in the database

## User Stories

1. As a cashier using POS, I want to select an existing customer or leave it blank for walk-in sales
2. As a cashier using POS, I want to add parts from catalog via barcode scan or search
3. As a cashier using POS, I want to create special (ad-hoc) products when item not in catalog
4. As a cashier using POS, I want to add labor services with hourly time tracking
5. As a cashier using POS, I want to add bicycle line items referencing templates
6. As a repair technician, I want optional customer on repair intake for walk-in repairs
7. As a repair technician, I want CRUD line items on repairs incrementally
8. As a salesperson, I want optional customer on orders for walk-in orders
9. As a salesperson, I want atomic parts/labor/bicycle line items when creating order
10. As a salesperson, I want optional customer on quotes for anonymous estimates
11. As a salesperson, I want CRUD line items on quotes incrementally
12. As a developer, I want shared CustomerSelector component used by all modules
13. As a developer, I want shared line item variant definitions in one file
14. As a shop owner, I want every part sold to reference catalog entry

## Implementation Decisions

### Module 1: Shared Customer Selector Component (Frontend)
- Extract from POS into `client/src/features/customers/components/CustomerSelector.tsx`
- Props: `{ customerId?: string | null, onSelect, required?: boolean }`
- All four modules import and use this component

### Module 2: Shared Line Item Variant Definitions (Shared Validations)
- Create `shared/validations/line-item-variants.ts` with part/labor/bicycle variants
- Each module composes its own discriminated union from shared variants

### Module 3: Customer Optional Across All Modules (Backend Schemas)
- Repairs: allow customerId null without existing/new customer path
- Orders: customerId changed to nullable optional
- POS/Quotes already optional — no change

### Module 4: POS Service Layer Upgrade (Backend)
- `createDirectSale()` handles labor and bicycle line items
- Stock validation only on part-type items

### Module 5: POS Cart Store Upgrade (Frontend)
- Cart supports discriminated union of all three line item types
- Cart display renders appropriate fields per type

## Testing Decisions

1. Shared Customer Selector — unit tests for selection callback, null handling
2. Line Item Variant Schemas — unit tests for each variant valid/invalid inputs
3. POS Sales Service — integration tests: parts-only, labor, bicycle, mixed-type cart
4. Orders Schema — unit test customerId optional

## Out of Scope

1. Line item UI components (parts/labor/bicycle sections) — deferred to later pass
2. Fixed-price labor services — hourly stays core
3. Bicycle inventory management — templates only
4. Inline customer creation at POS — walk-in only
5. Multi-payment split, invoicing, void auth guard

name: tdd
description: Test-driven development with red-green-refactor loop. Use when user wants to build features or fix bugs using TDD, mentions "red-green-refactor", wants integration tests, or asks for test-first development.
---

# Test-Driven Development

## Philosophy

**Core principle**: Tests should verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't.

**Good tests** are integration-style: they exercise real code paths through public APIs. They describe _what_ the system does, not _how_ it does it. A good test reads like a specification - "user can checkout with valid cart" tells you exactly what capability exists. These tests survive refactors because they don't care about internal structure.

**Bad tests** are coupled to implementation. They mock internal collaborators, test private methods, or verify through external means (like querying a database directly instead of using the interface). The warning sign: your test breaks when you refactor, but behavior hasn't changed. If you rename an internal function and tests fail, those tests were testing implementation, not behavior.

See [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.

## Anti-Pattern: Horizontal Slices

**DO NOT write all tests first, then all implementation.** This is "horizontal slicing" - treating RED as "write all tests" and GREEN as "write all code."

This produces **crap tests**:

- Tests written in bulk test _imagined_ behavior, not _actual_ behavior
- You end up testing the _shape_ of things (data structures, function signatures) rather than user-facing behavior
- Tests become insensitive to real changes - they pass when behavior breaks, fail when behavior is fine
- You outrun your headlights, committing to test structure before understanding the implementation

**Correct approach**: Vertical slices via tracer bullets. One test → one implementation → repeat. Each test responds to what you learned from the previous cycle. Because you just wrote the code, you know exactly what behavior matters and how to verify it.

```
WRONG (horizontal):
  RED:   test1, test2, test3, test4, test5
  GREEN: impl1, impl2, impl3, impl4, impl5

RIGHT (vertical):
  RED→GREEN: test1→impl1
  RED→GREEN: test2→impl2
  RED→GREEN: test3→impl3
  ...
```

## Workflow

### 1. Planning

When exploring the codebase, use the project's domain glossary so that test names and interface vocabulary match the project's language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

Before writing any code:

- [ ] Confirm with user what interface changes are needed
- [ ] Confirm with user which behaviors to test (prioritize)
- [ ] Identify opportunities for [deep modules](deep-modules.md) (small interface, deep implementation)
- [ ] Design interfaces for [testability](interface-design.md)
- [ ] List the behaviors to test (not implementation steps)
- [ ] Get user approval on the plan

Ask: "What should the public interface look like? Which behaviors are most important to test?"

**You can't test everything.** Confirm with the user exactly which behaviors matter most. Focus testing effort on critical paths and complex logic, not every possible edge case.

### 2. Tracer Bullet

Write ONE test that confirms ONE thing about the system:

```
RED:   Write test for first behavior → test fails
GREEN: Write minimal code to pass → test passes
```

This is your tracer bullet - proves the path works end-to-end.

### 3. Incremental Loop

For each remaining behavior:

```
RED:   Write next test → fails
GREEN: Minimal code to pass → passes
```

Rules:

- One test at a time
- Only enough code to pass current test
- Don't anticipate future tests
- Keep tests focused on observable behavior

### 4. Refactor

After all tests pass, look for [refactor candidates](refactoring.md):

- [ ] Extract duplication
- [ ] Deepen modules (move complexity behind simple interfaces)
- [ ] Apply SOLID principles where natural
- [ ] Consider what new code reveals about existing code
- [ ] Run tests after each refactor step

**Never refactor while RED.** Get to GREEN first.

## Checklist Per Cycle

```
[ ] Test describes behavior, not implementation
[ ] Test uses public interface only
[ ] Test would survive internal refactor
[ ] Code is minimal for this test
[ ] No speculative features added
```
